interest: A disabled Americans' periodical asked whether Japan exterminated the disabled; Dickover explained Japanese family-based welfare.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.145/12-2044) centers on an inquiry sent in December 1944 to newly appointed Under Secretary of State Joseph C. Grew by Melvin E. Schoonover, the youthful editor and publisher of The Shut-In's Companion in Monon, Indiana. Schoonover sought information regarding the treatment, education, and institutional care of crippled and physically handicapped persons in Japan, asking whether the Japanese government practiced eradication comparable to Nazi Germany or neglected the disabled. Enclosed with his letter was a complete copy of the December 1944 Christmas issue (Vol. 2, No. 3) of The Shut-In's Companion, containing inspirational essays, staff biographies of disabled contributors, poetry, and advertisements. In January 1945, Erle R. Dickover, Chief of the Division of Japanese Affairs, replied on Grew's behalf, explaining that the closely knit Japanese family unit historically assumed primary responsibility for disabled members rather than the state, though recent years had seen the Ministry of Welfare establish limited public and private institutions. Dickover also provided an extensive reference bibliography of English-language books, periodicals, and official Japanese government reports on social welfare.

subfiles.about: Inquiry from Melvin E. Schoonover congratulating Joseph C. Grew on his appointment as Under Secretary of State and requesting information on government policies and care for handicapped persons in Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter from Melvin E. Schoonover to Joseph C. Grew

subfiles.about: The December 1944 issue of The Shut-In's Companion, an inspirational monthly magazine published for physically disabled individuals and shut-ins.
subfiles.summary: The full twelve-page December 1944 Christmas issue (Vol. 2, No. 3) of The Shut-In's Companion, published at Monon, Indiana, and sponsored by the Indiana Society for Crippled Children, enclosed with Schoonover's letter to Grew. The issue contains holiday editorials, biographical sketches of disabled staff members, book reviews, short fiction, poetry, humor, and reader correspondence. Highlights include Isabel Currier's article 'Careers for the Handicapped' detailing the founding of Rehabilitation Associates, Inc., a multi-million-card greeting business established by paralyzed individuals in Boston, as well as a 'Curious Facts' column mentioning limb regeneration in frogs and Japanese seppuku (hara-kiri).
subfiles.title: The Shut-In's Companion, Vol. 2, No. 3 (December 1944)

subfiles.about: State Department reply from Erle R. Dickover explaining the Japanese family unit's responsibility for the disabled and the emerging role of the Ministry of Welfare.
subfiles.summary: Dickover tells Schoonover that care of the disabled in Japan traditionally rests with the family, though welfare institutions are growing, and encloses a bibliography.
subfiles.title: Letter from Erle R. Dickover to Melvin E. Schoonover
